I can't argue that 2 is correct, because I don't think it is. The matching framing in the solution is right, but the expectation it leads to is 138/55 ≈ 2.51.

Debater A's argument has two problems.

First, the denominator argument doesn't establish anything. A reduced fraction with denominator 35 doesn't show that a Markov-chain calculation is correct, and "a wrong answer would more likely have a messier denominator" is not evidence. The 138/55 value also has a clean denominator, so this heuristic can't separate the two.

Second, the method is only as good as its execution, and Debater A's own note concedes that 144/35 hasn't been checked numerically. A rough estimate suggesting about 3 also doesn't support 144/35 (≈ 4.11). It doesn't support 2 either.

The direct calculation: N equals the sum of ⌊L/2⌋ over the maximal runs of equal ranks, which is the number of cards at even positions within their run. With f(k) the probability that k specific positions share a rank, f(2)=3/11, f(3)=3/55, f(4)=1/165, and f(5)=0. Summing the even-position probabilities gives 3/11 + 12/55 + 9·(37/165) = 138/55.

I recommend a Monte Carlo simulation over random 12-card arrangements. It should give a mean near 2.51, which would rule out both 2 and 144/35.
